item.title: From additives to whole foods: why dietary policy is right to pivot
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor, The findings by Hasenböhler et al. linking intake of several food additive preservatives to increased cancer risk represent more than an incremental epidemiological signal [1]. item.title: Preservatives and cancer: Whole-food guidance need not wait for causal certainty
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor, Wang and Giovannucci appropriately emphasise caution in interpreting the modest associations between preservative intake and cancer risk, rightly calling for further validation before drawing causal conclusions [1]. However, the significance of the Hasenböhler et al. findings lies less in the confirmed carcinogenicity of individual additives than in what they reveal about the limits of an additive-by-additive approach to dietary safety [2]. item.title: High impact medical journals are not immune to industrialised manuscript fabrication
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor, Scancar and colleagues report a BERT-based screen that flags nearly one in ten cancer research articles as textually similar to retracted paper-mill papers, with the signal rising sharply over time and appearing even in high impact journals (1). item.title: Pancreatitis reports with GLP-1 receptor agonists require contextual interpretation
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor The MHRA’s strengthened warning on acute pancreatitis associated with glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonists is appropriate from a pharmacovigilance perspective. item.title: Positive predictive values are sensitive to specificity
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor, Scancar and colleagues report a BERT-based text classifier trained on retracted “paper mill” papers and controls. They apply it to a corpus of 2.65 million PubMed-indexed cancer research articles, of which it flags 261,245 (9.87%) with a reported accuracy of 91% as potential paper mill publications. item.title: Re: The impact of skin tone on performance of pulse oximeters used by NHS England COVID Oximetry @home scheme: measurement and diagnostic accuracy study
item.description: Agreement: I AgreeBody: Dear Editor The graph in the paper version of the BMJ was very useful for comparing the different pulse oximeters. However, for those of us with red green colour vision deficiency (8% of men in the UK) it was very difficult to interpret. Please could you consider using markers of different shape (e.g. squares, circles, triangles, stars) on graph lines to help us? Thanks. item.title: Reliability is not just a clinician trait when access is unpredictable
